values.value: Field notes from the team on the Model Context Protocol — what it is, why it earns its place in our toolchain, and what we have learned wiring it into real work.

value.markup: The Model Context Protocol is a small idea with a large blast radius: give every tool the same way of describing itself, and assistants stop needing a bespoke integration for each one. These posts are what we tell people who ask why we dropped everything to adopt it.

documents.name: Why MCP Is Awesome
documents.path: WWW / Blog / Why MCP Is Awesome

values.value: One protocol, and suddenly every tool in your stack speaks the same language. Here is why the Model Context Protocol changed how we wire assistants to real systems.

value.markup:
The first time an assistant reached into our issue tracker without anyone writing a line of glue code, the room went quiet. That is the moment MCP stops being a specification and starts being infrastructure.

Before MCP, every tool meant a new integration: a new auth flow, a new schema, a new set of prompts explaining how the thing worked. Multiply that by the number of tools a team actually uses and you get an impossible maintenance bill. MCP collapses all of it into one contract.

values.value: The old world: a screen full of one-off glue code. Photo: Chris Ried / Unsplash

value.markup:
Three things make it stick. Portability — a server written for one assistant works with the next one that walks through the door. Scope — you decide exactly which tools a given client may touch, so the scary ones stay behind a permission. And speed of delivery — a useful server is an afternoon, not a sprint.

None of that is magic. It is the payoff for choosing a boring, well-specified protocol over a clever proprietary one.

The part people underestimate is the blast radius on the boring work. Status pings, draft posts, changelog entries, the weekly report — all of it becomes a call instead of a chore, and all of it lands in the same audit trail.

Once the tools are on the protocol, the interesting question stops being "can the assistant do this?" and starts being "should it?". That is a much better conversation to be having.

values.value: We stopped budgeting for integrations and started budgeting for ideas.

documents.name: One Protocol, Every Tool
documents.path: WWW / Blog / One Protocol, Every Tool

values.value: Before MCP every integration was a one-off. Now a server you write on Monday works with every assistant on Tuesday. A look at what that means for day-to-day work.

value.markup:
The promise of MCP is unglamorous and that is exactly why it works: a server exposes what it can do, a client asks for it, and both sides agree on the shape of the conversation. No plugin marketplaces, no vendor handshake, no per-assistant packaging.

We noticed the change first in review meetings. Instead of arguing about which assistant to buy, we were writing small servers — an afternoon each — and letting every assistant in the company use them.

values.value: Two sides, one shape: pieces only fit when they were made to. Photo: Vardan Papikyan / Unsplash

value.markup:
The numbers surprised us. Our first server — read-only access to the CMS content store — took less than a day including tests. The second took an hour, because the hard decisions had already been made once.

That is the compounding part. The protocol is the same every time, so the learning lives in your team instead of in each integration.

We also got a security story we could actually explain. Every server declares its tools, every client declares its scopes, and the whole exchange is visible in one log. Nothing hides inside a prompt.

Compare that with the alternative, where the only way to know what an assistant can reach is to ask it and hope the answer is honest.

values.value: One contract, written down once, and every assistant we have ever tried just works with it.
